A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work despite the change from PCSM to HPM and the new title. The default implementation, benchmarks and retained results can be matched reliably. Text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable in both versions.

before.justification: v1 reports original PCSM results on nine PDE problems, together with resolution-generalization experiments, training-data comparisons and calibration ablations.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results under the HPM name and reports additional coupling, inference-time, head-count, model-capacity and resolution-generalization results.

M1.justification: The preferred HPM implementation retains PCSM's softmax gates multiplied by Laplace–Beltrami basis functions, spectral projection and multi-head processing. Section 3.2 adds additive and direct concatenation coupling alternatives. These are limited component extensions; the generic coupling formulation and renaming do not establish a replacement of the default algorithm.

E1.justification: The same nine PDE datasets and physical domains remain. v2 Appendix A.4/Table 12 extends Airfoil coverage to upsampling from a model trained at 111 × 26 to evaluation at 221 × 51, alongside downsampling. This adds a resolution-transfer scenario without adding a dataset or PDE task.

E2.justification: Comparator membership matches across the corresponding benchmark, training-data and resolution comparisons. SpecSolver is the renamed PCSM without calibration, rather than a new baseline. The added analyses use the existing Transolver and fixed-spectral comparators.

E3.justification: v2 substantially extends the evaluation design with inference timing on an RTX 3090 at batch size 1, head-count controls from 1 to 16, a four-layer versus eight-layer capacity comparison, and training at intermediate Airfoil resolution for bidirectional transfer testing. These are additional protocols; the original benchmark splits, relative-L2 metric and training configurations remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New analyses examine inference overhead, sensitivity to head count, whether gains persist with fewer parameters, and generalization in both resolution directions. The coupling study replaces the earlier spectral-coefficient input ablations with additive and concatenation comparisons while retaining sigmoid and global-pooling contrasts. Existing frequency-count, convergence, modulation-pattern and fixed-basis-design analyses are retained or relocated.

E5.justification: The uncertainty entries in Tables 1–2 are retained unchanged. Neither version supplies additional run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests. New supplementary results use point estimates, consistent with the earlier ablation reporting practice.

E6.justification: The main benchmark scores remain unchanged, but substantial supplementary results are added. Table 6 reports inference times of 14.8, 30.9 and 17.4 ms for SpecSolver, Transolver and HPM. Tables 10–12 add head-count, reduced-capacity and resolution-transfer outcomes; the new HPM upsampling error is 1.57e-2 under the newly specified training resolution. Coupling-result entries are replaced, Table 3 gains a training-resolution row, and the fixed-baseline value changes from 5.31e-3 in v1 Table 5 to 5.33e-3 in v2 Table 7.

T1.justification: v2 introduces a claimed universal-approximation theorem in Section 3.3 and an integral-kernel derivation in Appendix A.1, including assumptions about dense sampling and continuous, bounded coupling functions. It also formalizes spectral and linear-attention special cases. v1 provides transform equations but no corresponding theorem or proof.

C1.justification: v1 presents pointwise calibration as a way to combine spectral priors with attention-like adaptability. v2 advances the broader central claim that HPM unifies spectral and attention methods as special cases and supports interactions beyond either approach. Its abstract also adds a claim of computational-efficiency superiority while retaining the accuracy and generalization claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations that performance gains arise from architecture rather than parameter count, that performance is relatively insensitive to multi-head count, and that softmax helps through competition between frequencies. The existing boundary-detail, layerwise modulation and generalization explanations remain largely intact, as do the stated limitations concerning basic coupling design and unexplored applications.

D1.justification: v2 newly identifies PaddlePaddle, documents the RTX 3090 timing setup and parameter counts, and changes the advertised code link from PCSM to HPM. The main hyperparameter table is unchanged. Some reproducibility detail is lost: v1 specifies the exact early, middle and late layer indices for fixed-frequency enhancement, whereas v2 does not.

R1.justification: The positioning shifts from a gated spectral-calibration method to a framework encompassing spectral operators and linear attention. Related work expands to continuum attention, operator pretraining and additional spectral approaches, while the dedicated neural-gate discussion is removed. The comparison with AFNO and incremental spectral learning is expanded to distinguish objectives, processing stages and potential complementarity.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and much of the methodology are substantially rewritten around HPM terminology and the unified formulation. Background and related work move before the methodology, coupling comparisons enter the main text, and convergence analysis moves to the appendix. Author order, affiliations and publication-header text also change.

P2.justification: The main text changes from a single-column preprint layout to a two-column proceedings layout. v2 adds a conceptual overview figure, redraws and combines architecture and basis illustrations, reorganizes Table 1 by method family, and adds several experimental tables. Convergence and resolution-error figures move to the appendix, while most underlying heatmaps are retained.

improvement.justification: The timing, capacity controls, coupling comparisons and additional resolution tests strengthen validation of the retained method. However, the new universal-approximation assurance is not established by the supplied appendix: Appendix A.1.2 derives an integral-kernel representation without a universality argument and treats Project, including nonlinear LayerNorm, as a learned matrix without justification. The added empirical evidence is useful, but the stronger unsupported theoretical assurance creates a material tradeoff, leaving the net change in overall quality uncertain.
